accepted_examples.german: In jener Nacht war es schrecklich kalt.
accepted_examples.english: That night was terribly cold.
accepted_examples.note: Schrecklich is correctly used adverbially and translated as terribly.

accepted_examples.german: Sind Sie bereit, ein kleines Zugeständnis zu machen, um Ihr Ziel zu erreichen?
accepted_examples.english: Are you willing to make a small concession in order to achieve your goal?
accepted_examples.note: Erreichen is used for achieving a goal; both the German and English express that meaning.

accepted_examples.german: Sie führten den Befehl des Kapitäns präzise aus.
accepted_examples.english: They carried out the captain's order to the letter.
accepted_examples.note: Befehl is the captain’s order, and ausführen means to carry it out; the translation matches.

accepted_examples.german: Du hast am selben Tag Geburtstag wie ich.
accepted_examples.english: Your birthday is the same as mine.
accepted_examples.note: Geburtstag means birthday; the sentence and translation are accurate.

accepted_examples.german: Sie setzte ihre Haut nicht der Sonne aus.
accepted_examples.english: She didn't expose her skin to the sun.
accepted_examples.note: Haut means skin in the sentence, and the translation is direct.

accepted_examples.german: Darauf würde ich an deiner Stelle nicht wetten.
accepted_examples.english: I wouldn't bet on that if I were you.
accepted_examples.note: Wetten is used as bet on that; the sentence is grammatical and the translation matches.

accepted_examples.german: Tom sah traurig aus dem zerbrochenen Fenster.
accepted_examples.english: Tom looked sadly out of the broken window.
accepted_examples.note: Traurig is used adverbially with aus etwas sehen and is translated as sadly.

accepted_examples.german: Ich warte auf einen wichtigen Anruf.
accepted_examples.english: I'm waiting for an important phone call.
accepted_examples.note: Anruf means a phone call; the translation preserves the meaning.

accepted_examples.german: Es ist Zeit für die Nachrichten auf Kanal 79.
accepted_examples.english: It's time for the news on Channel 79.
accepted_examples.note: Nachrichten is used for the news broadcast; both language pairs match.

accepted_examples.german: Ich will einfach nur etwas Ruhe und Frieden.
accepted_examples.english: What I want is some peace and quiet.
accepted_examples.note: Frieden is used in the sense peace; Ruhe und Frieden is idiomatic and correctly translated.

accepted_examples.german: Bitte führen Sie Ihre Karte ein!
accepted_examples.english: Please insert your card.
accepted_examples.note: Karte means a card inserted into a device; this is a clear example of the card sense.

accepted_examples.german: Ich weiß Ihre Güte zu schätzen.
accepted_examples.english: I appreciate your kindness.
accepted_examples.note: Güte means kindness in this formal but natural sentence.

accepted_examples.german: Ich fürchte, diesmal kann ich dich nicht retten.
accepted_examples.english: I'm afraid I can't save you this time.
accepted_examples.note: Diesmal means this time; the sentence and translation agree.

accepted_examples.german: Das ist zu persönlich.
accepted_examples.english: That's too personal.
accepted_examples.note: Persönlich is used predicatively in the sense personal/private; the English is accurate.

accepted_examples.german: Die Sonne gibt Licht und Wärme.
accepted_examples.english: The sun gives light and heat.
accepted_examples.note: Sonne is used as the ordinary noun sun; the translation is exact.

accepted_examples.german: Der Professor schien in Gedanken versunken zu sein.
accepted_examples.english: The professor seemed to be lost in thought.
accepted_examples.note: Professor is used for the academic title; the sentence and translation match.

accepted_examples.german: Die Testergebnisse eines Lügendetektors sind vor Gericht unzulässig.
accepted_examples.english: The results of a lie detector test are inadmissible in court.
accepted_examples.note: Gericht is used in the legal sense court, not the food sense; the translation makes the sense clear.

accepted_examples.german: Die Katze hielt die Nase in den Topf.
accepted_examples.english: The cat put its nose in the pot.
accepted_examples.note: Nase means nose and is used literally; the translation matches.

accepted_examples.german: Ich weiß nicht, ob Tom gut singen kann.
accepted_examples.english: I don't know whether Tom can sing well or not.
accepted_examples.note: Singen is the infinitive after können and correctly means sing.

accepted_examples.german: Er ist mit irgend etwas beschäftigt.
accepted_examples.english: He is busy doing something.
accepted_examples.note: Beschäftigt is used with mit in the sense busy/occupied; the translation matches.

accepted_examples.german: Tom hat vor, einen neuen Computer zu kaufen.
accepted_examples.english: Tom is going to buy a new computer.
accepted_examples.note: Computer means computer; the sentence is grammatical and the translation is direct.

accepted_examples.german: Es war offensichtlich, dass es keinen Ausweg gab.
accepted_examples.english: It was apparent that there was no way out.
accepted_examples.note: Offensichtlich means apparent/obvious and introduces a dass clause correctly.

held_examples.reason: The candidate uses Punkt to mean exactly/on the dot, not the entry’s punctuation-mark sense.

held_examples.german: Du hast dich in letzter Zeit sehr verändert.
held_examples.reason: The source sentence uses verändert as a verb participle, but this entry is the adjective changed/altered.

held_examples.german: Mußt du jeden Tag zu Fuß zur Schule?
held_examples.reason: Zu Fuß means on foot; the entry sense is the body part, so use a direct body-part example.

editorial_examples.german: In der Abkürzung steht ein Punkt.
editorial_examples.english: There is a period in the abbreviation.
editorial_examples.note: The candidate uses Punkt to mean exactly/on the dot, not the entry’s punctuation-mark sense.

editorial_examples.german: Nach der Renovierung sah das Zimmer völlig verändert aus.
editorial_examples.english: After the renovation, the room looked completely changed.
editorial_examples.note: The source sentence uses verändert as a verb participle, but this entry is the adjective changed/altered.

plural_reviews.note: For the substantivized adjective meaning a stranger, the nominative plural is Fremde; weakly declined forms use Fremden.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Nominative plural: Fremde; weakly declined cases use Fremden.

plural_reviews.note: Both Komas and the learned variant Komata are listed for the coma sense.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Komas is the common learner form; Komata is a learned variant.

plural_reviews.note: The German plural is Countys; the English counties form is not used in German.
Queens is the plural for countable queens; the specific royal title is normally singular.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Queen is usually a title in this sense; Queens is used when referring to multiple queens.

plural_reviews.note: Eimer has an unchanged plural.

plural_reviews.value: No plural for table salt; Salze for distinct chemical compounds.
plural_reviews.note: Duden marks kitchen salt without a plural, while Salze is used for chemical compounds.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Table salt is normally singular; Salze refers to chemical types.

plural_reviews.note: Tropfen has an unchanged plural in the drop sense.
Maus forms Mäuse.
Charaktere is the plural for characters/personality types; it is distinct from the abstract sense of character.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Use Charaktere for individual characters or types.

plural_reviews.note: Staffel forms Staffeln in the season sense.
For the nautical crow’s-nest/platform sense, Wiktionary records masculine Mars → Marse and feminine Mars → Marsen.
plural_reviews.usage_note: The nautical term varies by grammatical gender: der Mars → Marse; die Mars → Marsen.

plural_reviews.note: The feminine technical noun Media is distinct from mass-media usage. For communications the usual German plural is Medien (from Medium); Mediä is a technical plural form of Media.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Technical noun: Mediä/Medien. For mass communications, use die Medien (plural of das Medium).

plural_reviews.note: Zelt forms Zelte.
As a count noun for an expression or token of thanks, Dankeschön forms Dankeschöns.
Keks forms Kekse.
Penisse is the usual plural; Penes is a learned/technical variant.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Penisse is usual; Penes is a learned variant.

plural_reviews.note: Boys is the German plural for the loanword Boy.
Nebel is unchanged in the plural.
Duden lists both Blutdrücke and Blutdrucke for the medical sense.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Both forms are recorded; the singular is more common when discussing a person’s blood pressure.

plural_reviews.note: Hühnchen is a diminutive in -chen and has an unchanged plural.
Praxis forms Praxen.
Heroinnen is the plural for female heroes; it is unrelated to das Heroin, the drug.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Female hero: Heroinnen. Do not confuse with das Heroin (drug).

plural_reviews.note: For a 45-rpm record, Single forms Singles.
Husten is a possible plural for this masculine noun but is rare; the illness is ordinarily discussed in the singular.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Rare plural; normally used in the singular.

plural_reviews.note: Bargelder exists for distinct cash holdings/sums but is uncommon; ordinary cash is a mass noun.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Rare, mainly financial use; normally singular in everyday speech.

plural_reviews.value: Usually singular in this fast-paced action/events sense.
plural_reviews.note: For the mass/event sense, the everyday German noun Action is normally singular; the source candidate itself marks this sense as usually singular.

plural_reviews.value: Usually singular as a collective noun for livestock.
plural_reviews.note: Vieh is a collective noun for livestock and is normally singular; Viecher can be colloquial/pejorative and is not the neutral plural.
plural_reviews.usage_note: Collective noun, normally singular; Viecher is colloquial/pejorative.

plural_reviews.note: Wodka forms Wodkas when referring to types or servings.
Werkstatt forms Werkstätten.
Fußball forms Fußbälle for the sport/game ball sense.

entry_updates.value: Media (technical): a voiced consonant or the middle layer of a blood or lymph vessel; mass-media communications are usually Medien
entry_updates.note: The entry has the feminine article die, which corresponds to the technical German noun Media. The English gloss “media” alone can mislead readers into treating it as the ordinary mass-media term; clarify that the ordinary communications word is Medien, plural of Medium.
